title: The Covenant Between the Pieces
summary: God answers Abram’s fear with a promise of countless offspring, credits his faith as righteousness, and seals the land promise by passing between the pieces.
historicalContext: The chapter follows directly on Abram’s night raid against the eastern coalition and his refusal of Sodom’s spoils (14:13-24). He is a resident alien in Canaan, rich in flocks and servants yet landless and, after roughly a decade in the land, still without a son (12:4; 16:3). Household customs of the second millennium explain his reasoning, for a childless master could designate a trusted servant as heir. The ritual of cutting animals and setting the halves opposite each other belongs to the world of ancient covenant-making, where binding oaths were sealed over slain animals and the oath-taker might pass between the pieces; Jeremiah 34:18-19 shows that Judah still knew the practice centuries later. The prophecy then reaches forward to Israel’s sojourn and bondage, the judgment on Egypt, the Exodus with great substance, and the conquest of a land held by ten peoples whose iniquity was not yet full.
literaryContext: Genesis 15 stands at the hinge of the Abraham story. It gathers the two strands of the call in 12:1-3, seed and land, and treats each in a matching scene. Both scenes open with a divine self-declaration (“I am thy shield,” v. 1; “I am the LORD that brought thee out,” v. 7), continue with Abram’s respectful question to the “Lord GOD” (vv. 2, 8), and close with a sign: the stars for the seed, the fire between the pieces for the land. Verse 6, the narrator’s verdict on Abram’s faith, binds the halves together. Shared vocabulary ties the chapter to chapter 14 (shield and delivered, substance, covenant), the prophecy of verses 13-16 anticipates Exodus, and the formula of verse 7 foreshadows Exodus 20:2. Chapter 16 then shows how quickly human impatience can test a promise so solemnly confirmed.
themes: God as shield and reward of the fearful
The promised seed from Abram’s own body
A covenant guaranteed by God alone
Divine patience and the timing of judgment
The land promise and the inheritance of the earth

outline.title: Shield, Stars, and Saving Faith
outline.summary: God reassures the fearful Abram, rejects Eliezer as heir, shows him the stars, and credits his trust in the promise as righteousness.

outline.title: The Land Promised and the Ritual Prepared
outline.summary: The Lord restates the land promise, Abram asks for assurance, and he prepares divided animals for a covenant ceremony, guarding them through the day.

outline.title: Prophecy in the Darkness
outline.summary: In a deep sleep Abram learns of four centuries of sojourn and affliction, the judgment of the oppressor, his own peaceful death, and God’s patience with the Amorites.

outline.title: God Passes Between the Pieces
outline.summary: Fire and smoke pass alone between the pieces as the Lord binds himself by covenant to give Abram’s seed the land of ten nations.

verses.bibleText: After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“After these things” ties the vision to the aftermath of chapter 14. Abram has just routed four eastern kings with a household militia, rescued Lot, received Melchizedek’s blessing, and refused the king of Sodom’s goods down to a thread and a sandal strap. A victory of that kind could invite retaliation, and the refusal of booty left him poorer than he might have been. Into that exposed moment comes “the word of the LORD … in a vision,” a formula that later heads the messages of the prophets and appears here for the first time in Scripture. Abram receives God’s word as a prophet would, and Genesis later calls him one (20:7).

“Fear not” is the first thing God says. Throughout Scripture the nearness of God unsettles those who meet him, and reassurance often comes before the message (Daniel 10:12; Luke 1:13). Abram’s fear is wider than awe, though. He has enemies who might return, a promise that has not yet produced a son, and years slipping past. God does not begin by removing those circumstances. He begins by naming himself in relation to Abram: “I am thy shield.”

The shield picks up Melchizedek’s blessing, which praised the God who had “delivered” Abram’s enemies into his hand (14:20); the two Hebrew words sound alike. The God who handed the kings to Abram will stand between Abram and every future threat. The second phrase answers the forfeited spoils. Abram declined Sodom’s wealth so that no one could say a pagan king had made him rich, and now the Lord takes responsibility for his reward. The Hebrew can be read “thy reward shall be exceeding great,” or, as the KJV has it, with God himself as the reward. The two readings stand together: the gift is great because the Giver is present in it, and nothing a king of Sodom could offer would match it.

The order of the scene matters for every later believer. Before Abram voices a question, God speaks; before any child is born, God offers himself. Faith in this chapter grows from a word addressed to a frightened man, and the protection promised does not hang on Abram’s skill in battle. The psalmists would take up the same picture of the Lord as shield (Psalm 3:3; 84:11), and Paul gathers it into one question: “If God be for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary word for the small round shield carried by a warrior, used often in the Psalms for God’s guarding care (Psalm 18:2; Psalm 28:7). Its sound echoes the verb in 14:20, where Melchizedek blessed the God who had “delivered” (miggen) Abram’s enemies. The link is a wordplay rather than proof of a shared meaning; its point is that the God who gave the past victory now pledges future protection.

wordNotes.term: שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד (sekharekha harbeh me’od) — thy exceeding great reward
wordNotes.explanation: Sakhar usually means wages or pay for work done, including a soldier’s compensation after a campaign (Ezekiel 29:19). Since Abram had just refused the spoils of war, the word is pointed. Harbeh me’od intensifies it: “very greatly.” The Hebrew most naturally reads “your reward will be very great,” while the KJV joins the phrase to “I am.” Psalm 127:3 calls children a sakhar from the Lord, a hint of the son Abram is about to ask for.

verses.bibleText: And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
For the first time in the narrative Abram answers God aloud. Until now the Lord spoke and Abram obeyed without recorded words (12:1-4; 13:14-18). His reply begins with an address found here for the first time, “Lord GOD,” combining the title of a master with the covenant name. He speaks as a servant before his sovereign even while laying a complaint before him. Lament and trust belong together in this conversation; Abram carries his disappointment to the One who made the promise instead of nursing it elsewhere.

“What wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless?” A great reward means little to a man with no one to receive it after him. The verb “go” pictures life as a journey, the same journey that began when he left Haran, and he is walking it without a son. “Childless” is a stark word, used elsewhere of those whose family line is cut off (Leviticus 20:20; Jeremiah 22:30). Years have passed since the first promise of 12:2, and Sarai is still barren (11:30).

The steward of his house is “this Eliezer of Damascus.” The Hebrew phrase behind “steward” is obscure, but verse 3 makes its sense plain: this man stands to inherit. Household law in Abram’s world allowed a childless master to designate a trusted servant as heir, who would care for him in old age, bury him, and receive the estate. Eliezer is not disparaged; he may well be the faithful servant of chapter 24 who prayed for a bride for Isaac. The grief lies in what Eliezer is not: a son of Abram’s own body through whom the promised nation could come. Abram can see only the customary solution, and he tells God so plainly.

wordNotes.explanation: Adonai means “my Lord,” the respectful address of a servant to a master. It is joined here to the divine name, which the Hebrew text points to be read as “God” so that “Lord” is not said twice; the KJV signals this with “Lord GOD.” The pairing returns in verse 8 and becomes a form of address in earnest prayer (Deuteronomy 9:26; Jeremiah 32:17).

Literally “son of mesheq,” a phrase found only here. Its exact meaning is uncertain; it may form a wordplay with Dammesheq, “Damascus,” which follows. Ancient translators took it as the one in charge of the household or the one who would possess it, and Abram’s restatement in verse 3 confirms that he means the heir. Proverbs 17:2 shows that a capable servant could share an inheritance among the sons.

verses.bibleText: And Abram said, Behold, to me thou hast given no seed: and, lo, one born in my house is mine heir.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram repeats himself, which in Hebrew narrative often signals strong feeling. Verse 2 described his condition; verse 3 names its cause. “To me thou hast given no seed” puts “to me” first for emphasis and names God as the One who has not yet given. The word “seed” reaches back to the promises of 12:7 and 13:15-16, where the land was pledged to Abram’s seed, and further back to the Seed of the woman in 3:15. Without seed, every other promise stalls.

“One born in my house is mine heir” describes Eliezer’s legal standing, not descent from Abram. A servant born in the household belonged to it and, lacking a son, could receive its inheritance. Abram is not in revolt. He is reasoning from what he can see toward the only arrangement he can imagine, and honest faith often sounds like this. The psalmists show that God’s people may ask “How long?” without being cast off (Psalm 13:1-2). God does not rebuke Abram; he answers with a sharper promise, and the next verse shows that the Lord had a solution Abram could not supply.

wordNotes.explanation: A collective noun for offspring, able to denote a single descendant or a great many. Genesis uses it from 3:15 onward to trace the line of promise. Paul draws on the singular form when he identifies the promised Seed ultimately with Christ (Galatians 3:16), while Abram’s countless descendants also remain in view (Genesis 13:16).

verses.bibleText: And, behold, the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And, behold” marks a sudden turn. The word of the LORD comes again and interrupts Abram’s calculations with a flat denial: “This shall not be thine heir.” God does not even repeat Eliezer’s name. The arrangement Abram had resigned himself to is set aside, not because Eliezer was unworthy, but because God meant to give what custom could not.

“He that shall come forth out of thine own bowels” is the language of physical descent; the heir will be Abram’s own son. The mother is not yet named, and the next chapter shows Abram and Sarai filling that silence with a scheme of their own (16:1-4). Only in 17:16-19 is Sarah named as the mother. God’s promises often arrive in stages, and the gaps between them test whether his people will wait for the next word or hurry ahead with human devices.

The same expression returns in God’s promise to David, of offspring that “shall proceed out of thy bowels” (2 Samuel 7:12), a word that reached its fulfillment in the Son of David. The phrase in Genesis 15 links the birth of Isaac to the longer line that leads to Christ, the Seed in whom Abraham’s blessing reaches the nations and through whom believers become Abraham’s heirs (Galatians 3:29).

wordNotes.term: מִמֵּעֶיךָ (mimme‘ekha) — out of thine own bowels
wordNotes.explanation: Me‘im denotes the inward parts and, by extension, the source of procreation (Genesis 25:23; Isaiah 48:19). The phrase insists on a son of Abram’s own body rather than an adopted heir. It reappears in the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12), so the two covenants share the language of a God-given descendant.

verses.bibleText: And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God brings Abram “forth abroad,” out of the tent and into the night. The vision has been unfolding indoors; now Abram is shown the sky. “Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them.” The task is impossible by design. Under the clear sky of the Judean hills, with no light but the stars, their number seems endless, and the command makes Abram feel the limits of his own reckoning.

“So shall thy seed be.” In 13:16 the comparison was the dust of the earth; now it is the host of heaven. Both images defy measurement, but the stars add something. They are the work of God’s word (Psalm 33:6; Isaiah 40:26), each called by name and upheld by his power (Psalm 147:4). The One who numbers the stars can give a son to an old man and a barren wife. The sign turns Abram’s eyes from the promise to the might of the Promiser.

The scene also shows how God strengthens faith. Abram receives no new evidence about his own body or Sarai’s; nothing on earth has changed. He receives a renewed word and a picture drawn from creation. Moses would later tell Israel that they had become as the stars of heaven for multitude (Deuteronomy 1:10), and Hebrews recalls that from one man “as good as dead” came descendants beyond counting (Hebrews 11:12). Paul saw the promise reach further still, to all who share Abraham’s faith from every nation (Romans 4:16-18). Every clear night became a sermon Abram could hear again.

wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of safar, “to count.” The KJV’s “tell” keeps the older English sense of counting. The verb is used again when Jacob recalls the promise of seed that cannot be numbered for multitude (Genesis 32:12), and the great multitude which no man could number in Revelation 7:9 echoes the same patriarchal hope.

verses.bibleText: And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator now steps out of the dialogue to comment. The verb form is not the usual chain of narrative sequence, which suggests a summary of Abram’s settled response more than a single event at that moment. Abram had already trusted God when he left Ur and Haran (Hebrews 11:8); here Scripture names that trust and records God’s verdict on it. “He believed in the LORD”: the object is the Lord himself, who had just promised a son beyond natural possibility.

The Hebrew verb comes from the root that also gives “amen.” It means to regard something as firm and reliable and to rest one’s weight on it. Such faith is personal reliance on God’s word when sight offers no support. Paul describes the same act when he says that Abraham considered his own body now dead, yet was fully persuaded that God was able to perform what he had promised (Romans 4:19-21).

“And he counted it to him for righteousness.” The Lord is the one who reckons. Righteousness elsewhere describes a life that measures up to God’s standard (Ezekiel 18:5-9), and Abram had no such record of his own; Genesis has already shown his deception in Egypt (12:11-20) and will show more. God credits to Abram a standing he had not earned, and Abram receives it by trusting the promise. The verb belongs to the language of accounts: something is entered to a person’s credit. Psalm 32:2 uses it of the blessed man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity, and Paul sets the two texts side by side (Romans 4:3-8).

This is the first place in Scripture where faith and righteousness are joined, and the timing carries Paul’s argument. Abram was counted righteous before circumcision (chapter 17) and centuries before the law at Sinai, and so he stands as father of all who believe, whether Jew or Gentile (Romans 4:9-12; Galatians 3:6-9). His faith was no meritorious achievement that bought God’s favour. It was the empty hand that received a gift.

Nor did that faith stay idle. The same Abraham later obeyed when told to offer Isaac, and James cites Genesis 15:6 as fulfilled in that obedience (James 2:21-23). The righteousness credited by grace bore fruit in a life that kept God’s commandments (26:5). In Abram’s story justification and obedience are partners: the first is God’s gift received by faith, and the second is the growth of a heart that has learned to rest on him. Every sinner who looks to Christ, the promised Seed, is welcomed on the same terms.

wordNotes.explanation: The Hiphil of ’aman, “to be firm, reliable.” In this stem the verb means to hold someone trustworthy and rely on him; followed by “in the LORD,” it expresses personal trust. This is its first occurrence in the Bible. Isaiah plays on the same root when he warns that those who will not believe will not be established (Isaiah 7:9). The Greek Old Testament renders it with the verb Paul quotes in Romans 4:3.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה (vayyachsheveha lo tsedaqah) — he counted it to him for righteousness
wordNotes.explanation: Chashav means to reckon, account, or impute. With “to him” and a predicate noun it describes crediting something to a person’s account, whether guilt (2 Samuel 19:19) or righteousness (Psalm 106:31). Tsedaqah is right standing and right conduct measured by God’s standard. The Greek Old Testament puts the verb in the passive, “it was reckoned to him,” the form quoted in Galatians 3:6. The initiative lies with God: he pronounces the verdict, and Abram receives it.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second scene opens with a fresh self-declaration, and some interval of time is implied. The first vision came under the stars; this one moves through a day toward sunset (vv. 12, 17). “I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees” reminds Abram that his journey began with God’s initiative. Joshua 24:2-3 recalls that Abram’s family served other gods beyond the river, so his departure from Ur was a rescue from idolatry as well as a migration (Nehemiah 9:7).

The wording anticipates the preface to the Ten Commandments, where the Lord names himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 20:2). In both places a past act of deliverance grounds what follows. At Sinai redemption comes before law; here the call from Ur comes before the covenant oath. Grace takes the first step, and the response God seeks is shaped by what he has already done.

The purpose clause is plain: “to give thee this land to inherit it.” This is the third statement of the land promise (12:7; 13:14-17). Abram has walked its length and breadth, yet he owns none of it; even a grave for Sarah will have to be bought (23:4, 16). Stephen observed that God gave him no inheritance in it, “not so much as to set his foot on” (Acts 7:5), and Hebrews explains that Abraham looked for a city with foundations, built by God (Hebrews 11:9-10). The promise was real and earthly, and it was also larger than any plot Abram could have occupied in his lifetime.

wordNotes.explanation: From yarash, “to take possession, inherit.” The same root supplied “heir” in verses 3-4, so the questions of son and land are joined: the one who inherits from Abram will inherit the land. In settings of conquest yarash often means to possess by dispossessing the present occupants (Deuteronomy 9:1), which prepares for the mention of the Amorites in verse 16. Jesus applies the inheritance language to the meek, who shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).

verses.bibleText: And he said, Lord GOD, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram’s reply mirrors verse 2. Again he says “Lord GOD,” and again he asks a question: “whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?” Coming directly after the narrator’s statement that he believed, the question must be heard as the asking of a believer. Abram does not doubt God’s willingness. He asks for a pledge that he and his descendants could hold when the promise seemed most remote.

Scripture records requests for signs that God honours and others he rebukes. Gideon sought confirmation and received it (Judges 6:36-40); Hezekiah asked for a sign of his healing (2 Kings 20:8). Zacharias met the angel’s announcement with unbelief and was struck dumb (Luke 1:18-20), while Mary’s “How shall this be?” was answered with explanation (Luke 1:34-35). The difference lies in the heart behind the words, which God alone reads. Abram’s request falls on the side of faith seeking assurance.

God’s answer is a covenant ceremony, with no reproach attached. He stoops to forms Abram would recognise and binds himself in the solemn manner of the age. Hebrews reflects on the same willingness: wanting the heirs of promise to be fully confident, God confirmed his word by an oath (Hebrews 6:17-18). Believers who struggle for assurance are free to ask, and the answer God gives always directs them to the reliability of his own commitment.

wordNotes.term: בַּמָּה אֵדַע (bammah eda‘) — whereby shall I know
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “by what shall I know?” The expression asks for a token or evidence, as when Moses asked how it would be known that God’s people had found grace in his sight (Exodus 33:16). Abram’s verb “know” is answered in verse 13 by God’s emphatic “know of a surety,” so the chapter itself shows the Lord meeting the request with sure knowledge.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God answers the request for knowledge with instructions: “Take me an heifer … a she goat … a ram … a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” The word “me” signals that the animals are brought for the Lord. Every species named belongs to the list later appointed for Israel’s offerings: cattle, goats, and sheep from the herd and flock, and turtledoves or young pigeons as the offering of the poor (Leviticus 1:2, 14; 5:7). Long before Sinai, Abram handles the very creatures the sanctuary would use to teach the meaning of atonement.

Each of the larger animals is “of three years old,” mature and at full strength. The detail shows that God asks for the best, not the weak or the leftover. Heifer, goat, and ram also figure in later rites of purification and atonement (Numbers 19:2; Leviticus 16:5), so the collection gathers the chief kinds of sacrificial victim into one scene.

No altar is built and Abram kindles no fire. The ritual is a covenant ceremony rather than a burnt offering, yet the choice of sacrificial animals gives it a sacrificial character. Covenants in Scripture are ratified with the life of a victim, as Sinai was ratified with blood (Exodus 24:8), and the New Testament explains that the new covenant was sealed by the death of Christ (Hebrews 9:15-18). Abram understood little of this. He obeyed anyway, gathering the animals without being told what would happen next.

wordNotes.explanation: A participle formed from the numeral “three,” literally “threefold.” Some ancient interpreters took it as “three of each kind,” but most translations read it as an age. The same form describes the “threefold cord” of Ecclesiastes 4:12. Animals of three years were full-grown, fitting the later rule that what is offered to God be without defect (Leviticus 22:21).

wordNotes.term: תֹּר וְגוֹזָל (tor vegozal) — a turtledove, and a young pigeon
wordNotes.explanation: Tor is the turtledove; gozal is a nestling or young bird (Deuteronomy 32:11). Together they anticipate the birds allowed in Israel’s offerings, especially for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:8). Mary and Joseph brought this offering of the poor when Jesus was presented in the temple (Luke 2:24).

verses.bibleText: And he took unto him all these, and divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided he not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram does as he is told, and more than the recorded words told him: he “divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another.” Verse 9 says nothing about cutting, so either Abram received fuller instruction or he recognised the form of a covenant ritual from the customs of his world. The halves were laid opposite each other with a path between, while the birds were left whole, perhaps because of their size, as later law also directed (Leviticus 1:17).

The Hebrew idiom for making a covenant is literally “to cut a covenant” (v. 18), and this scene shows the practice behind the phrase. Ancient treaty texts describe animals slain when oaths were ratified, at times with the explicit statement that a faithless party would suffer the fate of the animal. Jeremiah 34:18-19 gives the clearest biblical parallel: the leaders of Judah who passed between the parts of a calf and then broke their word would be handed over to their enemies. To walk between the pieces was to call down a curse on oneself: may I be torn apart like these if I fail to keep this oath.

Abram may well have walked the path between the carcasses as he arranged them, as covenant custom would suggest, but the narrative fixes attention elsewhere. It records his obedience and his labour and then waits for the decisive moment when another will pass through (v. 17). The patience of the scene teaches its own lesson. Abram prepares what God requires and then waits through the day for God to act, without presuming to complete the covenant himself.

The divided animals also foreshadow a weightier truth. The curse of covenant-breaking must fall on someone, whether the unfaithful party or a substitute. The whole sacrificial system rested on the principle that a life given stands in for a life forfeited (Leviticus 17:11), and that principle reached its fulfilment when Christ was made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb batar, “to cut in two,” is used in the Old Testament only in this verse. The related noun bether, “piece,” recurs in verse 17 and in Jeremiah 34:18-19, the only other passage describing a covenant made between divided animals. The rarity of the vocabulary underlines how solemn and unusual the ceremony was.

verses.bibleText: And when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away.” Birds of prey descend quickly on carrion in open country, and the detail shows that hours passed between the preparation and God’s appearing. Abram stands guard over the pieces and will not let the offering be torn apart before the Lord comes. The act is practical, yet it is also reverent and persistent: he keeps what has been laid out for God intact while he waits.

Birds of prey were unclean in Israel’s later law (Leviticus 11:13-19), and elsewhere in Scripture they picture hostile powers that swoop on their victims (Isaiah 46:11; Ezekiel 17:3). Because the prophecy that follows speaks of Abram’s descendants afflicted in a foreign land, many readers see in the scene a picture of threats against the promised people, with Abram defending what God has pledged, much as he had just rescued Lot from foreign kings. The text does not interpret the birds, so such readings are best held lightly.

Faith often looks like this verse: waiting for God with a heavy heart while warding off whatever would spoil what has been offered to him. Distraction, discouragement, and temptation can descend like birds on an altar. Abram drives them off and keeps watch until the Lord appears, and the prophet would later urge the same patient vigilance for a vision that tarries (Habakkuk 2:3).

wordNotes.explanation: A collective term for birds of prey such as vultures and kites that swoop on carcasses. Isaiah uses it for the conqueror God summons from the east (Isaiah 46:11), Jeremiah for predators gathering against God’s heritage (Jeremiah 12:9), and Ezekiel for the birds that feed on fallen enemies (Ezekiel 39:4).

verses.bibleText: And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When the sun was going down” marks the passage of time. The night vision under the stars has given way to a day of preparing and watching, and evening is coming on. As the light fades, “a deep sleep fell upon Abram.” The word is the one used when the Lord caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam before forming Eve (2:21). In both places the sleep is God’s doing, setting the man aside while God acts and speaks. Later recipients of revelation fall into a similar state (Job 4:13; Daniel 10:9).

With the sleep comes “an horror of great darkness.” This is the only place in the story where Abram is overwhelmed with dread in God’s presence, and no sin of his has prompted it, as it had when Adam hid in the garden. The darkness readies Abram for the message he is about to hear: before the promise is fulfilled, his descendants will pass through a long night of oppression. Exodus would later describe a darkness that could be felt falling on Egypt when God judged the oppressor (Exodus 10:21-22).

The covenant God offers no easy optimism. He shows Abram the cost and the delay ahead before he passes between the pieces, and faith that is grounded in such candour can survive the dark, because it was told beforehand that darkness would come. Jesus likewise warned his disciples of tribulation so that, when it arrived, they would remember his words and take courage, because he had overcome the world (John 16:33).

wordNotes.explanation: A heavy sleep brought on by God, distinct from ordinary rest. It fell on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and on Saul’s camp, where it is said to be “from the LORD” (1 Samuel 26:12). In Job 33:15 it is the setting in which God speaks to people in a vision of the night, which fits its use here as the moment of revelation.

wordNotes.term: אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה (’emah chashekhah gedolah) — an horror of great darkness
wordNotes.explanation: ’Emah is terror or dread, often the fear that God’s presence or mighty acts produce (Exodus 15:16; Exodus 23:27). Chashekhah is darkness, intensified here by “great.” The phrase may describe dread that consists of thick darkness or dread that accompanies it; either way the atmosphere anticipates the gloom of bondage and the terror God would later send on Israel’s enemies.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not their's, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Know of a surety” answers Abram’s question of verse 8 with the strongest form Hebrew can use, the verb “know” doubled. Abram wanted knowledge, and God gives it, though not the knowledge he might have chosen. Before the inheritance comes a long sojourn: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not their’s, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years.”

Three stages are named: sojourning as aliens, servitude, and affliction. The land is left unnamed, and history supplied the name. Abram’s descendants lived as strangers in Canaan and then in Egypt; Jacob served Laban, Joseph was sold as a slave, and at last Israel groaned under Egyptian taskmasters (Exodus 1:11-14). The verb “afflict” is the one Exodus uses for that oppression. Stephen summarised this very prophecy in his defence before the council (Acts 7:6-7).

The “four hundred years” must be read with Exodus 12:40-41, which gives 430 years for the sojourning, and Galatians 3:17, which counts 430 years from the covenant with Abraham to the law. The most coherent reading counts the 430 years from Abram’s call at seventy-five (12:4) to the Exodus, including the years in Canaan as well as in Egypt, and the ancient Greek translation of Exodus 12:40 already reads it that way. The 400 years of affliction would then begin some thirty years after the call, around the time Isaac was weaned and mocked by Ishmael, which Paul calls persecution (21:8-10; Galatians 4:29). On that reckoning about half the period was spent in Canaan and half in Egypt. A round figure in prophecy and a precise one in retrospect are not at odds.

Whatever reckoning one prefers, the weight falls on the certainty and sovereignty of God’s word. He knows the length of his people’s trial before it begins, and he sets its limit. Suffering lies within his foreknowledge and does not cancel his promise. Believers who wait through long afflictions can take heart that the God who numbered Israel’s years in bondage also holds their times in his hand (Psalm 31:15).

wordNotes.term: יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע (yadoa‘ teda‘) — know of a surety
wordNotes.explanation: An infinitive absolute followed by the finite verb, literally “knowing, thou shalt know,” a Hebrew way of stressing certainty. The warning “thou shalt surely die” is built the same way (Genesis 2:17). The expression picks up Abram’s “whereby shall I know” in verse 8 and answers it with God’s guarantee.

A resident alien who lives among a people not his own without the rights of a native. Abraham called himself a ger among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), and Israel’s experience as strangers in Egypt became the ground of later laws protecting the stranger (Exodus 22:21; Deuteronomy 10:19). Hebrews applies the identity to all the faithful who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Hebrews 11:13).

verses.bibleText: And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The prophecy turns from bondage to judgment: “that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge.” God does not name Egypt, but he binds himself to act against the oppressor. The plagues fulfilled this word. The Lord told Moses he would redeem Israel “with great judgments” (Exodus 6:6), and on the night of the Passover he executed judgment against all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12).

“And afterward shall they come out with great substance.” The word for substance is the one used for the goods taken and recovered in chapter 14. Abram had refused to be enriched by Sodom; God now promises that his descendants will leave slavery richly supplied, receiving from the Egyptians what amounted to long-withheld wages (Exodus 12:35-36). The Lord who would not let a pagan king make Abram rich makes Abram’s children rich at the end of their servitude.

The pattern of affliction, judgment on the oppressor, and deliverance with abundance recurs through Scripture and reaches its climax in the final deliverance of God’s people. The redeemed in Revelation sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb, praising the God whose judgments are just and true (Revelation 15:3). The Exodus foretold to Abram in the darkness became the template for every later act of redemption, including the one accomplished by Christ.

wordNotes.term: דָּן אָנֹכִי (dan anokhi) — will I judge
wordNotes.explanation: Din means to judge, both to give a verdict and to carry it out, often on behalf of the oppressed (Psalm 72:2). The emphatic pronoun anokhi, “I myself,” stresses that God will act in person. Rachel later named a son Dan, “judge,” in thanks that God had judged her cause (Genesis 30:6).

Movable property: goods, livestock, and wealth. It describes Abram’s possessions when he left Haran (Genesis 12:5) and the goods seized and recovered in the war of chapter 14 (Genesis 14:16). Its use here links Abram’s experience with Israel’s: God, not the king of Sodom, enriches his people.

verses.bibleText: And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
In the middle of the national prophecy God speaks to Abram personally: “thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age.” Abram will not see the bondage or the Exodus. He will live out a full span and die at peace. The promise was kept. Abraham died “in a good old age, an old man, and full of years” at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah beside Sarah (25:7-10).

“Go to thy fathers” is one of several Hebrew expressions for dying, alongside being “gathered to” one’s people (25:8) and sleeping with one’s fathers (1 Kings 2:10). It does not describe a conscious soul passing into a realm where the ancestors are awake and waiting. Abram’s fathers had served other gods beyond the river (Joshua 24:2), and he would be buried in Canaan, far from their graves in Mesopotamia; the phrase places him with them in the common lot of death. The parallel line spells out its meaning: “thou shalt be buried.” Scripture consistently presents death as a sleep in which the dead know nothing (Psalm 146:4; Ecclesiastes 9:5), awaiting the resurrection.

That is why Hebrews says that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob “died in faith, not having received the promises” (Hebrews 11:13), and that the faithful of old will not be made perfect apart from believers of later times (Hebrews 11:39-40). Abraham sleeps in the dust with his hope intact. Jesus pointed to God’s title “the God of Abraham” as evidence for the resurrection, because God’s covenant with the patriarch guarantees that he will live again (Luke 20:37-38). The reunion that matters will come when the Lord descends and the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

The word “peace” also deserves notice. Abram will die reconciled, unafraid, and secure in God’s word, though he owns only a burial plot in the land. Such a death is a gift. Death remains an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), yet for the one who trusts God it is an enemy whose defeat is already assured.

wordNotes.term: תָּבוֹא אֶל־אֲבֹתֶיךָ (tavo el-avotekha) — thou shalt go to thy fathers
wordNotes.explanation: An idiom for dying, parallel to being “gathered to” one’s people (Judges 2:10) and sleeping with one’s fathers (2 Kings 10:35). The second half of the verse, “thou shalt be buried,” gives its concrete sense. Abraham was in fact buried at Machpelah in Canaan, far from his ancestors’ tombs, so the phrase speaks of sharing their death rather than their grave or a place where the dead are conscious (Psalm 146:4).

wordNotes.term: בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה (beseivah tovah) — in a good old age
wordNotes.explanation: Seivah means grey hair and hence old age. Old age alone can be bitter, as Jacob feared (Genesis 42:38); the adjective “good” marks it as full and blessed. The phrase is used of Abraham at his death (Genesis 25:8), of Gideon (Judges 8:32), and of David (1 Chronicles 29:28).

verses.bibleText: But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again.” The return is as certain as the bondage. The word for “generation” can denote a lifetime or a cycle of time, and here four such spans correspond to the four hundred years of verse 13. Traced through the genealogies, the fulfilment is also visible: Moses belonged to the fourth generation from Levi, through Kohath and Amram (Exodus 6:16-20). One generation went down into Egypt, two lived there, and a fourth came out. The text does not invite exact calculations of how long a generation lasts; its concern is certainty and limit.

Then comes the reason for the delay: “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.” The Amorites stand here for the whole population of Canaan (compare Joshua 24:15; Amos 2:9-10). God would not dispossess them while their probation continued. The land was not handed over at once, because its inhabitants still had time to turn, and because Israel was not yet a people able to occupy it.

The sentence lays bare the moral government of God. Judgment on nations is not arbitrary; it falls when wickedness has reached its full measure, as it did before the Flood (6:5-13) and would at Sodom (18:20-32). Moses later warned Israel that the Canaanites were being driven out for their abominations and that Israel too would be expelled if it copied them (Leviticus 18:24-28; Deuteronomy 9:4-5). The conquest under Joshua came as justice after centuries of forbearance.

The same patience marks God’s dealings with the world now. Peter explains the apparent delay of Christ’s return as longsuffering, since the Lord is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). There is a limit, and the measure of iniquity will be filled; until then the door of mercy stands open. Abram’s descendants waited so that the Amorites might have time, and the church waits so that more may be saved.

wordNotes.explanation: Shalem describes what is complete or whole. Here the iniquity has not yet reached completion, the point at which judgment falls. The wordplay with shalom, “peace,” in verse 15 is striking: Abram will die in peace, while the Amorites’ guilt moves toward its full measure. Jesus speaks in comparable terms when he tells the leaders of his day to fill up the measure of their fathers (Matthew 23:32), and Paul of those who fill up their sins (1 Thessalonians 2:16).

wordNotes.term: דּוֹר רְבִיעִי (dor revi‘i) — the fourth generation
wordNotes.explanation: Dor can mean a generation of people or a span of time roughly a lifetime long (Deuteronomy 23:3; Psalm 90:10 sets the ordinary life at seventy or eighty years, though patriarchal lives ran far longer). Paired with the four hundred years of verse 13, it describes four long lifetimes, and the genealogy of Moses traces the fourth generation from Levi (Exodus 6:16-20).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed between those pieces.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When the sun went down, and it was dark”: the scene that began at sunset now reaches full night. Out of the darkness appear “a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp,” and they pass “between those pieces.” The furnace is a firepot or portable oven trailing smoke; the lamp is a flaming torch. Smoke and fire mark God’s presence throughout Scripture: the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21), and Sinai wrapped in smoke because the Lord descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18). Abram now sees that presence in visible form for the first time.

The decisive feature is who passes through. In covenant custom the one who walked between the pieces called down on himself the fate of the slain animals should he break his word. Here God alone passes between them. Abram lies in a deep sleep and does not walk the path at the climax of the ceremony. The Lord takes the whole obligation on himself, pledging his own life that the promise of land and seed will stand. Hebrews draws out the logic: because God could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself, so that by two unchangeable things, his promise and his oath, the heirs of promise might have strong consolation (Hebrews 6:13-18).

The covenant is therefore a covenant of grace, secured by God’s own commitment. Abram’s faith receives it; his works do not establish it. His descendants were not thereby free to live as they pleased. Later covenants spelled out the obedience fitting for a redeemed people, and in chapter 17 God calls Abram to walk before him and be perfect. Yet the foundation of the relationship was laid here, with God binding himself to bring his word to pass.

The image presses toward the cross. If the ritual meant that the covenant-maker would be torn apart should the covenant fail, the repeated unfaithfulness of Abram’s descendants raised an urgent question: who would bear the curse? The gospel answers that God, in the person of his Son, took it on himself. Christ “hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us,” so that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles (Galatians 3:13-14). The fire moving between the pieces points to the God who would one day give himself for the covenant-breakers he had pledged to bless.

The fire may also have consumed the pieces, as fire from the Lord later fell on the sacrifices of Aaron and Elijah as a sign of acceptance (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38).

wordNotes.explanation: Tannur is a clay oven or firepot used for baking (Leviticus 2:4; Hosea 7:4). Joined with “smoke,” it calls to mind the column of smoke associated with the divine presence at Sinai. Isaiah speaks of the Lord whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem (Isaiah 31:9), using the same word for God’s burning presence among his people.

wordNotes.term: לַפִּיד אֵשׁ (lappid esh) — a burning lamp
wordNotes.explanation: Lappid is a torch or flame. It is used of Gideon’s torches hidden in pitchers (Judges 7:16) and of the flashes at Sinai, which the KJV renders “lightnings” (Exodus 20:18). Daniel saw a heavenly figure whose eyes were as lamps of fire (Daniel 10:6). Torch and smoking oven together picture the holy, consuming presence of God.

verses.bibleText: In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram.” This is the first use of the word covenant in the Abraham story, and the verb is literally “cut,” matching the ritual just completed. A day of fear, questions, waiting, and darkness ends with a binding oath. The promise is stated in the past tense: “Unto thy seed have I given this land.” Abram owns nothing yet, but God speaks as though the transfer has already taken place, because his word guarantees the outcome; he calls things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17).

The boundaries run “from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates.” The northern limit is clear, the southern debated. Elsewhere the border of Canaan is the “brook” of Egypt, usually identified with the Wadi el-Arish (Numbers 34:5), while here the word is “river,” which may point to an eastern branch of the Nile. Israel’s rule reached toward these limits under David and Solomon, when tribute came from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:21), but the nation never settled the whole territory.

The promise, then, outruns its partial fulfilment. The two great rivers recall the rivers that watered Eden (2:10-14), as though the land promised to Abram were a pledge of paradise restored. Paul states the matter directly: the promise to Abraham and his seed was that he should be “the heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). Jesus took up Psalm 37:11 when he said that the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and the Bible closes with a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1-3).

For Abram the covenant was both concrete and expansive. It secured a real land for a real nation, and its horizon reached to the earth made new, which Abraham will inherit at the resurrection together with all who share his faith (Galatians 3:29). The God who keeps time with the Amorites’ iniquity and Israel’s four generations will keep his word about the final inheritance as well.

wordNotes.term: כָּרַת בְּרִית (karat berit) — made a covenant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “cut a covenant,” the regular Hebrew idiom for concluding one, illustrated here by the divided animals of verses 10 and 17. Berit denotes a solemn, binding commitment, sometimes between equals and sometimes, as here, a pledge undertaken by the greater party. The same expression describes the new covenant promised through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31), which Hebrews sees fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:8).

A Hebrew perfect, ordinarily used for completed action. In promises God sometimes speaks of the future as already done because his word cannot fail. The verb natan, “give,” runs through the chapter: Abram complained that God had given him no seed (Genesis 15:3), and God now declares that he has given the land. Joshua later records that the Lord gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers (Joshua 21:43).

verses.bibleText: The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The land is now described by its inhabitants. Ten peoples are listed, more than the usual lists of six or seven (Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1), and the number probably conveys completeness: every people then in the land falls within the promise.

The first three names are the least known. The Kenites were a southern clan, later linked with Moses’ father-in-law and friendly to Israel (Judges 1:16; 1 Samuel 15:6). The Kenizzites may be connected with Caleb, who is called “the Kenezite” (Numbers 32:12). The Kadmonites, whose name means “eastern people,” appear only here. Some of these groups were later absorbed into Israel instead of being destroyed, a reminder that God’s dealings with the nations included mercy as well as judgment.

wordNotes.explanation: The name may relate to metalworking, as with Tubal-cain (Genesis 4:22), though the connection is uncertain. Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, belonged to this people (Judges 4:11), and Jael, who struck down Sisera, was the wife of a Kenite (Judges 4:17).

verses.bibleText: And the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Rephaims,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list continues with three more peoples. The Hittites, descended from Heth (10:15), were settled around Hebron, where Abraham would later buy Sarah’s burial cave from them (23:3-20). The Perizzites, whose name may refer to dwellers in unwalled villages, already lived alongside the Canaanites in Abram’s day (13:7).

The Rephaims, remembered for their great stature, had just been struck by the eastern kings (14:5) and were later associated with Og, king of Bashan, and his huge iron bedstead (Deuteronomy 3:11). Their place in the list shows that even formidable peoples could not stand in the way of God’s pledge.

wordNotes.explanation: A people of great stature whom neighbouring nations called by other names, such as Emim and Zamzummim (Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 2:20). Joshua mentions the land of the Rephaim in the wooded hill country (Joshua 17:15). Their presence in the promised land helps explain the fear of the spies who felt like grasshoppers before such giants.

verses.bibleText: And the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final four names complete the ten. The Amorites, already named in verse 16 as representative of the land’s moral condition, were a strong people of the hill country and of the region east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21-25). The Canaanites lived especially by the sea and along the Jordan valley (Numbers 13:29). The Girgashites are little known, and the Jebusites held Jerusalem until David captured it (2 Samuel 5:6-9).

The list ends where much of Israel’s later history would centre. The city of the Jebusites became Zion, the place of the temple. The God who named the nations then occupying the land looked centuries ahead to Jerusalem, where a greater Son of Abraham would offer the sacrifice that the divided animals foreshadowed and open the inheritance to every people that believes (Acts 3:25-26).

wordNotes.explanation: The people of Jebus, the older name of Jerusalem (Judges 19:10; 1 Chronicles 11:4). Their stronghold resisted Israel until David took it and made it his capital. Araunah the Jebusite later sold David the threshing floor on which the temple was built, a site identified with Mount Moriah, where Abraham would offer Isaac (2 Samuel 24:18; 2 Chronicles 3:1).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When God’s promises seem slow in coming, what do you do with your questions?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God meets fearful faith with his own word and oath, credits trust in his promise as righteousness, and binds himself alone to accomplish what he has spoken.
discussionQuestions: Why does God answer Abram’s fear first by naming himself rather than by changing his circumstances?
How do verses 2 and 8 show that honest questions can belong to faith rather than to unbelief?
What does Paul draw from the fact that Abram was counted righteous before circumcision and before Sinai?
What do the long delay and the iniquity of the Amorites reveal about God’s justice and patience?
Why is it significant that only the fire passed between the pieces?
commonMisunderstandings: Abram’s questions in verses 2 and 8 are not marks of unbelief; the narrator sets his faith squarely between them.
Faith is not a meritorious work that earns righteousness; God credits righteousness to the one who trusts his promise, and that faith goes on to obey.
To “go to thy fathers” does not teach that Abram’s conscious soul would join his ancestors; it is a Hebrew idiom for death and burial, with the inheritance awaiting the resurrection.
The conquest of Canaan was not arbitrary aggression; God delayed it for centuries until the iniquity of its peoples was full.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God’s initiative central: he speaks first, he credits righteousness, he swears the oath, and he alone passes between the pieces, while Abram’s part is to trust, to obey, and to wait.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring your fears and questions to the God who is your shield, rest your whole weight on his promise fulfilled in Christ, and wait for him with the patience of Abram.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Righteousness by faith: God credits righteousness to sinners who trust his promise, a promise fulfilled in Christ, and that faith bears the fruit of obedience.
flow: Abram had no righteousness of his own and no power to produce the promised heir.
God gave him a promise and invited him to look at the stars and trust the Creator.
Abram believed, and God counted that trust to him for righteousness.
God then bound himself by oath, alone passing between the pieces, pointing to Christ who bore the curse.
Everyone who believes in Christ is counted righteous in the same way and begins to walk in grateful obedience.
simpleIllustrations: A debt cancelled by another’s payment is entered on the debtor’s account as settled; the debtor receives the credit by accepting the payment, not by working off the balance.
A child who leans his full weight on his father’s arm across a stream shows what Abram’s word for belief means: resting on someone strong enough to carry you.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you, like Abram, rest your whole weight on God’s promise in Christ and receive the righteousness he freely credits to all who believe?
cautions: Do not present faith as a work that earns God’s favour; it is the empty hand that receives his gift.
Do not separate justification from the obedient life that faith produces (James 2:21-23).
Do not use the land promise to support political claims; the New Testament widens it to the heir of the world and the earth made new.

reflectionQuestions: What fears am I carrying that God answers first by reminding me who he is?
Am I bringing my honest questions to God, or nursing them away from him?
Where am I tempted, like Abram, to settle for the customary solution instead of waiting for God’s promise?
Do I rest on Christ’s righteousness credited to me, or am I still trying to earn my standing before God?
How does God’s patience with the Amorites shape the way I view his patience with me and with the world?
